Semantic Review in Your Harness

Source: vignettes/harness-semantic-review.Rmd
harness-semantic-review.Rmd

Use this guide when you want a model to judge the ontology candidates metasalmon found for your package, and you have supporting files such as README notes, data dictionaries, or technical reports for it to read.

metasalmon makes no model call and needs no API key. The judgement runs in your own harness, such as Claude Code or Codex: the package writes a review packet, the harness answers it, and the package reads the answers back and checks them. Nothing the harness answers reaches your metadata until you confirm it.

The route at a glance

  1. Create the package with create_sdp().
  2. Write a review packet with write_semantic_review_packet(), passing your supporting files as context_files.
  3. Have your harness judge the packet. The ready-made harness is the sdp-semantic-review skill of the smn-sci-plgn plugin.
  4. Read the answers back with ingest_semantic_assessments().
  5. Confirm each answer in the review_semantics() queue with accept_suggestion(), then write your decisions with apply_sdp_semantics().

Install the harness skill

The sdp-semantic-review skill ships in the public smn-sci-plgn plugin, from its v0.2.0 release. Install the plugin in Claude Code or Codex as its README describes. The skill reads the packet’s own instructions, chooses only from the candidates the packet offers, writes the answer file in the package’s 30-column contract, and hands the confirming calls back to you.

The skill can also build the packet and ingest the answers itself, through metasalmonpy. The two packages write and read the same packet, so you can equally build and ingest in R, as below, and use the skill only to judge.

If you would rather write your own harness, the Semantic Review in R guide shows the shape of one.

Create the package 

library(metasalmon)

data_path <- system.file("extdata", "nuseds-fraser-coho-2023-2024.csv", package = "metasalmon")
fraser_coho <- readr::read_csv(data_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

pkg_path <- create_sdp(
  fraser_coho,
  path = "fraser-coho-2023-2024-sdp",
  dataset_id = "fraser-coho-2023-2024",
  table_id = "escapement",
  check_updates = FALSE,
  overwrite = TRUE
)

create_sdp() searches the vocabularies and writes the top-ranked compatible candidates as REVIEW: drafts. Those drafts, and the slots it left blank, are what the packet asks your harness to judge.

Choose your context files

context_files accepts local files that add domain context to the review:

  • markdown and text notes: .md, .txt, .rst
  • delimited and structured text: .csv, .tsv, .json, .yaml, .yml
  • source and notebook files: .R, .Rmd, .qmd
  • HTML pages: .htm, .html
  • Word documents: .docx
  • PDF reports: .pdf, with the optional pdftools package
  • Excel workbooks: .xls, .xlsx, .xlsm, with the optional readxl package

The files are read on your machine, cut into overlapping chunks, and scored against each target, and the packet carries the best excerpts beside each target rather than the whole file. They are evidence for the judge only: the judge still has to choose from the shortlist find_terms() retrieved, and it never mints an IRI.

Pass the paths themselves, not files you have already read:

context_files <- c(
  "README.md",
  "methods-note.Rmd",
  "data-dictionary.xlsx",
  "technical-report.pdf"
)

Do not pass the result of readr::read_csv(), xml2::read_html(), an R Markdown reader, or another parsed object. A tibble or XML document is data in memory, not a path, and it is refused with an error. Use context_text when the context is already a character string.

A good bundle mixes a README, HTML export or methods note describing the dataset; a CSV, workbook, DOCX or R Markdown data dictionary or analyst note; and a technical report, if one exists. The package’s own metadata/column_dictionary.csv is a reasonable choice too.

Plain-text and CSV inputs are read as UTF-8. If they contain invalid UTF-8, metasalmon retries Windows-1252/Latin-1 decoding before the text is scored. R Markdown and HTML inputs are expected to be UTF-8. Each assessment records the files that supplied its excerpts in llm_context_sources. Files keep their base name; when two share one, the label adds the parent directory (and, if needed, a numeric suffix) so their excerpts stay distinct.

Write the packet 

packet <- write_semantic_review_packet(pkg_path, context_files = context_files)
packet$path      # <package>/review/semantic-review-packet.json
packet$packet_id # the SHA-256 the ingester checks

The packet holds exactly the slots review_semantics() would queue, each with its shortlist retrieved again (top_n = 5 by default) and the evidence the package’s validators read. Measurement columns are grouped into bundles, so the judge settles the whole variable (variable, property, entity, unit, constraint and statistical modifier) before deciding any one slot. It is written under review/, which no publication path reads.

Two arguments shape what the judge sees:

  • sources keeps the search inside a fixed set of vocabularies. Omit it for role-aware defaults; an explicit vector is a strict allowlist for the packet’s shortlists and for the one retry round a judge can ask for.
  • code_scope chooses which codes.csv values get a slot. The default, "factor", matches create_sdp(); a blank code slot it leaves out is listed in packet$not_covered rather than dropped silently.

Have your harness judge it

Open the package folder in your harness and ask it to review the packet at review/semantic-review-packet.json. The sdp-semantic-review skill writes its answers to review/semantic-assessments-pass-1.csv, and the packet’s packet_id to the one-line sidecar beside it, so the ingester can tell which packet it judged. Any harness has to do the same.

The judge answers every slot with one of five decisions:

  • accept: it picked a candidate from the shortlist, by index, and echoed its IRI.
  • review: it was not confident enough to pick; the slot is left for you.
  • retry_search: it asked for a better query. The package searches once more and writes a second packet for those slots only.
  • reject_shortlist: every candidate is the wrong concept family. The package escalates a rejection to request_new_term, so the gap is filed rather than lost.
  • request_new_term: a likely ontology gap. These rows are your cue to propose a new term rather than force a near miss.

Read the answers back 

result <- ingest_semantic_assessments(pkg_path)
result$status # "complete", or "awaiting_pass_2"

The ingester checks the answer file against the packet it names, then each row. An IRI the packet did not offer is recorded as an error and never applied, and a candidate index that is not a whole number is refused. Deterministic validators then check statistical-modifier and constraint evidence, role and ontology-type compatibility, known property and unit dimensions, and a small curated set of redundancy rules. A failed validator changes accept to review, clears the selection, and appends a stable finding code and its explanation; validators never substitute a term or create a gap. Free text the harness wrote is redacted of anything that looks like a credential before it is kept.

When status is "awaiting_pass_2", a retry found new candidates: have your harness answer review/semantic-review-packet-pass-2.json the same way, in semantic-assessments-pass-2.csv, and call ingest_semantic_assessments() again. There is no third pass.

The record is kept in review/semantic-llm-assessments.csv, one row per target in the 30-column assessment contract:

assessments <- semantic_llm_assessments(pkg_path)
assessments[, c("column_name", "dictionary_role", "llm_decision", "llm_confidence", "llm_selected_iri")]

Confirm and write your decisions

The ingester never touches the metadata CSVs. Each answer now sits in the review queue, under the candidate it chose:

review <- review_semantics(pkg_path)
review
# Paste the printed call for each answer you have checked, for example:
review <- accept_suggestion(
  review, "NATURAL_ADULT_SPAWNERS", "variable", rank = 1,
  table = "escapement"
)
apply_sdp_semantics(pkg_path, review)

Read each accepted definition against the column’s meaning before you accept it. A model’s choice and a passing validator are evidence, not a substitute for checking the source meaning. Semantic Review in R covers the queue, rejections and the metadata setters in detail.

Structured ontology gaps 

gaps <- detect_semantic_term_gaps(result$dictionary)

requests <- render_ontology_term_request(
  gaps,
  scope = "auto",
  ask = FALSE
)

detect_semantic_term_gaps() combines deterministic candidate gaps with the final request_new_term decisions your harness recorded. Its gap_detection_basis distinguishes candidate_gap, llm_request_new_term, and candidate_gap_and_llm_request_new_term, and a recorded gap stays visible even when SMN candidates exist. The post-review publication guide shows the gap table in detail.

Rendering never submits an issue. Routing precedence is an explicit row override, a forced scope, a recognized namespace the judge suggested, and then the placement heuristic. A suggested namespace is evidence rather than authority. Review every draft before using submit_term_request_issues().

Rebuild EDH XML after review

Once the package metadata is finalized:

validate_salmon_datapackage(pkg_path, require_iris = TRUE)
write_edh_xml_from_sdp(pkg_path)

write_edh_xml_from_sdp() refuses to rebuild from a package that still holds REVIEW: markers or unresolved dataset or table placeholders, so finish the review first.
